t: Count Non-Decreasing Subarrays After K Operations — Sliding Window with Monotonic Stack
o: The minimal number of increments to make nums[l..r] non-decreasing equals Σ max(0, max(nums[l..i−1]) − nums[i]): each element must be raised to the running prefix maximum. We must count subarrays whose cost ≤ k. Example 1: [6,3,1,2,4,4] with k=7 — the four subarrays starting at 0 with cost exceeding 7 are excluded, giving 21 − 4 = 17. Since n ≤ 10⁵ we need roughly linear time: a sliding window where the cost is maintained incrementally using a monotonic stack of compressed equal-value blocks.
k: Cost(l,r) = Σ max(0, prefixMax − nums[i]) over the subarray.
Adding an element on the right raises each existing block below its value; blocks merge into one.
Removing from the left decrements the front block and reduces the cost by (front.value − next.value).

a.n: Approach 1: Expand From Each Left Endpoint
a.i: Fix l and grow r, maintaining the running maximum and accumulated cost; stop as soon as the cost exceeds k, since cost only grows. This is the direct translation of the cost formula and very intuitive, though adversarial inputs make it quadratic.
s: For each l, scan r from l rightward keeping running max mx and cost.
Add max(0, mx − nums[r]) to cost, updating mx.
Count r while cost ≤ k; break otherwise.
a.t: O(n²) worst case (e.g., decreasing input lets every window extend far); fine for small inputs, too slow for n = 10⁵ extremes.

a.n: Approach 2: Sliding Window with Monotonic Stack of Blocks
a.i: Keep the window's lifted (non-decreasing) profile as blocks (value, count) in a monotonic stack, plus the current total cost. Adding x on the right pops all blocks with value ≤ x, adding (v − x)·count to the cost, then pushes merged block (x, total count). Shrinking from the left removes one unit from the front block, reducing the cost by (front.value − next.value). Both ends are amortized O(1), so the two-pointer window runs in linear time.
s: For each r, push nums[r]: pop blocks with value ≤ x, adding (v − x)·count to cost; push (x, merged count).
While cost > k, decrement the front block's count; if it empties, pop it, else subtract (front.value − next.value) from cost; advance l.
Add r − l + 1 to the answer.
a.t: O(n) — each element is pushed and popped from the monotonic structure at most once, and l only moves forward.
a.sp: O(n) for the block stack in the worst case (strictly increasing input).

w: Present the cost formula first — once the interviewer agrees cost(l,r) = Σ max(0, prefixMax − nums[i]), the sliding-window-with-blocks design follows naturally. Pitfalls: 64-bit accumulation (values up to 10⁹ × 10⁵ elements ≈ 10¹⁴), forgetting that the answer itself can exceed 32 bits (≈ 5×10⁹), and mishandling the front-block removal (subtract the gap to the next block per removed element, not per block). Edge cases: k ≥ total cost of the whole array (answer n(n+1)/2), all-equal arrays, strictly decreasing arrays. Follow-ups: count subarrays with cost exactly k, or handle decrement operations instead of increments.
